---
title: "Bilinear Forms and Matrix Representations"
---
\newcommand{\R}{\mathbf{R}}
\newcommand{\C}{\mathbf{C}}
\newcommand{\Q}{\mathbf{Q}}
\newcommand{\Hom}{\mathrm{Hom}}

In this section we discuss  bilinear forms over $\R$ and $\C$.  In some ways a bilinear form is a generalization of the notion of inner product, where we relax some of the conditions (such as symmetry or positive definiteness).  For a thorough discussion of this topic, see Keith Conrad's article [Bilinear Forms](https://kconrad.math.uconn.edu/blurbs/linmultialg/bilinearform.pdf).

In particular, we will consider only the case of vector spaces and bilinear forms over $\R$ or $\C$.  There are many interesting aspects of the theory over fields like $\Q$ or finite fields; see Conrad's notes for a discussion of this more general situation.

The definition doesn't depend on the field $F$, however. 

**Definition:** Let $F$ be a field and $V$ a vector space over $F$.  A bilinear form on $V$ is a function $B:V\times V\to F$ that is linear in each variable when the other is fixed.  In other words:

$$\begin{aligned}
B(au+v,w)&=aB(u,w)+B(v,w)\\
B(u,av+w)&=aB(u,v)+B(u,w)
\end{aligned}
$$

If $B(v,w)=B(w,v)$ for all $v,w\in V$, we call $B$ *symmetric*.  If $B(v,w)=-B(w,v)$ for all $v,w\in V$ we call $B$ *antisymmetric*  or *skew-symmetric*. If $B(v,v)=0$ for all $v$ we call $B$ *alternating.*

An inner product over a real vector space is a symmetric bilinear form.  This isn't true over a complex vector space, because we required such inner products to be *hermitian*. 

Other examples:

- If $A\in M_{n}(F)$, then $B(v,w)=v^{\top}Aw$ is a bilinear form.
- If $(u,v)$ and $(a,b)$ are in $F^{2}$, then 
$ub-va$ is a skew-symmetric bilinear form on $F^{2}$.

**Lemma:** Over $\R$ or $\C$ (or indeed any field of characteristic different from $2$), alternating forms are the same thing as skew-symmetric forms.

**Proof:** If $B$ is alternating, then
$B(x+y,x+y)=0=B(x,y)+B(y,x)$ so $B$ is skew-symmetric. If $B$ is skew-symmetric then
$B(x,x)=-B(x,x)$ so $2B(x,x)=0$, so $B$ is alternating assuming $F$ does not have characteristic two.

**From now on, every vector space is over $\R$ or $\C$.**

**Proposition:** Every bilinear form $B$ on $V$ is expressible uniquely as a sum 
$$
B(u,v)=B_1(u,v)+B_2(u,v)
$$
for all $u,v\in V$ where $B_1$ is symmetric and $B_2$ is skew-symmetric (alternating).

**Proof:**
Let 
$$
B_{1}(u,v) = \frac{B(u,v)+B(v,u)}{2}
$$
and
$$
B_{2}(u,v) = \frac{B(u,v)-B(v,u)}{2}.
$$
To see uniqueness, if $B=B_1+B_2=B_1'+B_2'$, then $B_1-B_1'=B_2'-B_2$.  The left side is symmetric, the right side alternating, so both sides are zero.


Finally, we have the *polarization identity*:
Suppose $B$ is symmetric.  Then
$$
B(x,y) = \frac{1}{2}(B(x+y,x+y)-B(x,x)-B(y,y))
$$

So a symmetric bilinear form is determined by its values $B(v,v)$ for all $v\in V$. 

### Orthogonality

We can generalize the notion of orthogonality from inner products to general bilinear forms by saying that $w \perp v$ when $B(w,v)=0$ and, more generally, that given a subspace $W\subset V$, then
$v\perp W$ provided $B(v,w)=0$ for all $w\in W$.

In general, this relation need not be symmetric; for a general bilinear form, one can have 
$B(v,w)=0$ (so $v\perp w$) but $B(w,v)\not=0$ so $w\not\perp v$.  For symmetric or alternating forms, however, the relation is symmetric since $B(v,w)=\pm B(w,v)$ for all $v,w\in V$ in these cases. 

One can show (see Conrad, Theorem 1.17 ([Bilinear Forms](https://kconrad.math.uconn.edu/blurbs/linmultialg/bilinearform.pdf)) that
$\perp$ is a symmetric relation if and only if $B$ is *either* symmetric or alternating.

If $B$ is symmetric or alternating, and $W\subset V$ is a subspace, then just as we did earlier with inner products we define
$$
W^{\perp} = \{ v\in V: v \perp w\quad \forall w\in W\} 
$$

Since it is quite possible, depending on $B$, for some nonzero vectors $v$ to be perpendicular to themselves,
one can have $W\cap W^{\perp}\not=0$.  For example if 
$B$ is the alternating form
$$
B((x,y),(u,v))=xv-yu
$$
on $F^{2}$, and $W$ is the span of $(1,1)$, then
$W^{\perp}=W$.  In fact every $v\in V$ is perpendicular to itself in this situation. 

Notice that if $W\subset V$ is a subspace, then the restriction of a bilinear form $B$ on $V$ is a bilinear form on $W$.  Also, if $V_1$ and $V_2$ are vector spaces with bilinear forms $B_1$ and $B_2$, then one can construct a bilinear form $B=B_1\oplus B_2$ on $V_1\oplus V_2$ by
setting
$$
B((x,y),(z,w))=B_1(x,z)+B_2(y,w).
$$

In this construction $V_1$ and $V_2$
are orthogonal in the sum, and so this sum is called the *orthogonal direct sum* of $B_1$ and $B_2$. Also, the restriction of $B$ to $V_1$ and $V_2$ recovers $B_1$ and $B_2$. 

### Bilinear forms and duality

Let $V$ be a vector space over $F$ with a bilinear form $B$.  For fixed $v\in V$, the map $f(w)=B(v,w)$ is a linear functional on $V$ and hence an element of the dual space $\Hom(V,F)$.  This gives a linear map 
$$
L_{B}: V\to \Hom(V,F).
$$

Alternatively we can fix $v\in V$ and define $g_{v}(w)=B(w,v)$.  This gives a map $R_{B}:V\to \Hom(V,F)$.  

**Proposition:** If $V$ is finite dimensional, and we identify $V$ with $\Hom(\Hom(V,F),F)$ then the two maps $L_{B}$ and $R_{B}$ are dual to one another.  In particular
$$
\hat{L}_{B}:V=\Hom(\Hom(V,F),F)\to \Hom(V,F)
$$
is the same as $R_{B}$ and vice versa.

**Proof:** This is a matter of keeping track of definitions.  If $v\in V$,
then the associated linear map from $\Hom(V,F)$ to $F$ is evaluation: $\delta_{v}:f\mapsto f(v)$.  Then
$$
\hat{L}_{B}(\delta_{v})=\delta_{v}\circ L_{B}
$$
But
$$
\hat{L}_{B}(\delta_{v})(w)=(\delta_{v}\circ L_{B})(w) = \delta_{v}(L_{B}(w))=L_{B}(w)(v) = B(w,v).
$$
Since $R_{B}(v)=B(\cdot, v)$, we have $R_{B}(v)(w)=B(w,v)$, so $\hat{L}_{B}(\delta_{v})=R_{B}(v)$.  The other duality follows similarly or via the fact
that $\hat{\hat{L}}_{B}=L_{B}=\hat{R}_{B}$.

### The Matrix of a Bilinear Form

Given a bilinear form on (finite dimensional) $V$, we can choose a basis $E=\{e_{1},\ldots, e_{n}\}$ for $V$.  Then $B$ is determined by the values $B(e_{i},e_{j})$ for $1\le i,j\le n$.  Let $M$
be the $n\times n$ matrix with these entries.  Then it's easy to see by linearity that
$$
B(v,w) = [v]_{E}^{\top}M[w]_{E}
$$

Conversely, given an $n\times n$ matrix, the formula above gives a bilinear form on $F^{n}$.  Thus we may
construct any bilinear form on $V$ by choosing a basis (an isomorphism with $F^{n}$) and an $n\times n$ matrix.

**Example:** Let $V=F^{n}$ and choose integers $p,q$ with $p+q=n$.  Let
$M$ be the matrix

$$
M = \left(\begin{matrix} I_{p} & 0 \\
0 & -I_{q} \end{matrix}\right)
$$

where $I_{k}$ is the identity matrix.  This creates a "pseudo-Euclidean space" with signature $p,q$.  If $p=3$ and $q=1$ we obtain Minkowski space, which is the flat spacetime of special relativity.

One can show (see Conrad, Theorem 2.5) that the matrix $M$ defined above is the
matrix of the linear map $R_{B}:V\to \Hom(V,F)$ relative to the choice of the basis $E$ on $V$ and its dual on $\Hom(V,F)$.  He uses this to give a "coordinate free" proof of the following facts:

1. $B$ is symmetric iff $M$ is symmetric.
2. $B$ is skew-symmetric (alternating) iff $M^{\top}=-M$.

One can also show (either in a fancy way as Conrad does, or by calculating)
that if $C$ is a change of basis matrix whose columns express the elements of a basis $E_{2}$ in
terms of $E_{1}$, 
and $B$ is a bilinear form on $V$ with matrix $M$ relative to $E_{1}$, then
the matrix of $B$ relative to $E_{2}$
is 
$$
M' = C^{\top}M C.
$$

If  $B_{2}$ is a bilinear form on $V_{2}$, and $L:V_{1}\to V_{2}$ is a linear map, then
$$
B_{1}(v,w)=B_{2}(Lv,Lw)
$$
is a bilinear form on $V_{1}$ (called the pullback of $B_{2}$ to $V_{1}$).

If we are given forms $B_{1}$ and $B_{2}$ on $V_{1}$ and $V_{2}$ respectively, then we say $B_{1}$ and $B_{2}$ are equivalent if there is a linear isomorphism from $V_{1}$ to $V_{2}$ so that the pullback of $B_{2}$ is $B_{1}$. 

In matrix terms, two bilinear forms $B_{1}$ and $B_{2}$ with matrix representations $M_{1}$ and $M_{2}$ are equivalent if there is an invertible matrix $C$ so that
$$
C^{\top}M_{1}C = M_{2}.
$$
